target.title: Generalizable spelling using a speech neuroprosthesis in an individual with severe limb and vocal paralysis

read.pdf: Figs. 1-6; Supplementary Figs. S1-S8; Supplementary Tables S1-S8 and Methods S1-S5 read

entries.text: The evaluation is a single-participant clinical-trial study; the participant was 36 at study start and had severe spastic quadriparesis and anarthria.
entries.condition: BRAVO clinical trial NCT03698149; one person with severe limb and vocal-tract paralysis; no independent participant cohort.
entries.quote: The participant, who was 36 years old at the start of the study, was diagnosed with severe spastic quadriparesis and anarthria

entries.text: Neural activity came from a 128-channel implanted ECoG array over sensorimotor cortex.
entries.condition: Single participant; 128 disk electrodes in a lattice at 4-mm center-to-center spacing; signals used for silent code-word classification and spelling.

entries.text: The spelling classifier used HGA from 70-150 Hz and LFS from 0.3-16.67 Hz after downsampling with anti-aliasing.
entries.condition: HGA and LFS feature streams, used jointly as HGA+LFS for real-time sentence spelling.
entries.loc: Results | Discriminatory content in high-gamma activity and low-frequency signals

entries.text: Signals were common-average referenced and each channel/feature type was z-scored using a 30-second sliding window; artifact rejection was also applied.
entries.condition: Real-time preprocessing of the ECoG feature streams before classification and detection.

entries.text: The speech detector was supervised with four time-point labels: rest, speech preparation, motor, and speech.
entries.condition: Detection-model training; only speech probability was used to engage the speller at use time.

entries.text: The speech-detection network used supervised learning with truncated backpropagation through time.
entries.condition: Continuous detection from HGA+LFS features; four labels during training.

entries.text: Real-time classifiers were trained using preceding-session data, with no day-of recalibration; each evaluation session used parameters fitted before that session.
entries.condition: Real-time sentence-spelling evaluation; classifier/model parameters and hyperparameters came exclusively from preceding sessions.
entries.loc: Results | Overview of the real-time spelling pipeline

entries.text: For sentence spelling, training also included data from prior sentence-spelling trials only when the decoded sentence had zero character errors.
entries.condition: Only preceding-session sentence-spelling trials were eligible; inclusion required exact decoded text.
entries.loc: Methods | Incremental classifier recalibration for sentence spelling

entries.text: The real-time letter classifier ensemble averaged predictions from 10 independently initialized models.
entries.condition: Same training dataset and architecture; differing random parameter initializations; predictions averaged per neural window.
entries.loc: Methods | Classifier ensembling for sentence spelling

entries.text: Isolated-target classifier evaluation used stratified 10-fold cross-validation, with 90% of each fold for training and 10% held out for testing.
entries.condition: Isolated-target task trials; one participant; stratified cross-validation.

entries.text: Within the training portion of each cross-validation fold, a stratified 10% subset was used as validation data.
entries.condition: Isolated-target cross-validation; validation data selected from the training partition.

entries.text: The letter classifier used a temporal convolution followed by two bidirectional GRU layers and a softmax over 27 labels.
entries.condition: Each input is a neural time window; outputs represent 26 NATO code words plus the hand-motor command.

entries.text: A silent-speech attempt volitionally engaged the speller; the user produced one code word at a paced go cue for each letter.
entries.condition: NATO phonetic code word represents each English letter; 2.5-second letter cycles.
entries.quote: attempted to silently spell using code words that represented the 26 English letters

entries.text: Each letter was decoded from a 2.5-second neural window immediately after the go cue.
entries.condition: Fixed-paced silent code-word production; 2.5-second, non-overlapping windows during sentence spelling.
entries.loc: Results | Overview of the real-time spelling pipeline

entries.text: An attempted right-hand squeeze ended spelling when its classifier probability exceeded 80%; the system then finalized the sentence.
entries.condition: Each 2.5-second classifier window; finalization removed incomplete words and rescored remaining candidates.
entries.quote: and if this probability was greater than 80%, the spelling procedure was stopped and the decoded sentence was finalized
entries.loc: Fig. 1 caption; Results | Overview of the real-time spelling pipeline

entries.text: A beam search used letter probabilities, automatically inserted spaces, and constrained candidate sentences to the 1,152-word vocabulary.
entries.condition: Real-time decoding; n-gram language-model prior during beam search; final rescoring occurred after hand-squeeze termination.
entries.quote: During real-time sentence spelling, the beam search only considered sentences composed of words from a predefined 1152-word vocabulary
entries.loc: Results | Overview of the real-time spelling pipeline

entries.text: The beam-search language model was a trigram; completed candidates were separately rescored with DistilGPT-2 at finalization.
entries.condition: The n-gram prior ranks word sequences during beam search; DistilGPT-2 rescoring uses only complete, in-vocabulary sentences at finalization.

entries.text: The authors report that classifier output was essential and that adding linguistic information improved sentence decoding beyond vocabulary constraints alone.
entries.condition: Offline omission simulations on the real-time copy-typing blocks; full real-time pipeline included beam search, vocabulary constraints, and language modeling.

entries.text: Copy-typing evaluation comprised 150 sentence trials: two attempts for each of 75 unique assistive-communication-corpus sentences.
entries.unit: trials; unique sentences; repetitions per sentence
entries.condition: Copy-typing task; 34 real-time blocks; target sentence displayed to the participant; 1,152-word vocabulary.
entries.quote: 150 sentences (two repetitions each of 75 unique sentences selected from an assistive-communication corpus

entries.text: Median character error rate for real-time copy-typing with the full language-model pipeline was 6.13%.
entries.condition: One participant; 150 copy-typing attempts of 75 unique sentences, 34 blocks; 1,152-word vocabulary; real-time full decoder with LM; 99% CI [2.25, 11.6].
entries.quote: We observed a median CER of 6.13%

entries.text: Median word error rate for real-time copy-typing with the full language-model pipeline was 10.53%.
entries.condition: One participant; 150 copy-typing attempts of 75 unique sentences, 34 blocks; 1,152-word vocabulary; real-time full decoder with LM; 99% CI [5.76, 24.8].

entries.text: 105 of 150 copy-typing sentences were error-free; 69 of 75 unique targets were decoded perfectly at least once across their two attempts.
entries.condition: Real-time copy-typing; 1,152-word vocabulary; full decoder with LM; two attempts per unique target.

entries.text: The decoded sentence contained the correct number of letters in 139 of 150 copy-typing attempts.
entries.condition: Real-time copy-typing; correct character count, supported by hand-squeeze termination classification.

entries.text: Median copy-typing speed was 29.41 characters per minute.
entries.condition: Real-time copy-typing, 34 blocks, 1,152-word vocabulary; 99% CI [29.1, 29.6].
entries.quote: We also observed a median CPM of 29.41

entries.text: Median copy-typing speed was 6.86 words per minute.
entries.condition: Real-time copy-typing, 34 blocks, 1,152-word vocabulary; 99% CI [6.54, 7.12].

entries.text: The highest observed real-time copy-typing block rates were 30.79 CPM and 8.60 WPM.
entries.condition: Maximum across individual copy-typing blocks, not the median; full real-time system with 1,152-word vocabulary.
entries.quote: spelling rates in individual blocks as high as 30.79 CPM and 8.60 WPM

entries.text: The authors report higher median spelling rates than the participant's commercial Tobii Dynavox device, with that device's benchmark measured in prior work.
entries.condition: Median commercial-device rates from the participant's previous-work measurement; 99% CIs [16.1, 19.3] CPM and [3.33, 5.05] WPM.

entries.text: Without vocabulary or language-model decoding, the neural classifier alone had median CER 35.1% and median WER 100%.
entries.condition: Offline copy-typing simulation using the top-probability character from each 2.5-second window; whitespace ignored; 99% CIs [30.6, 38.5] CER and [100.0, 100.0] WER.
entries.quote: This resulted in a median CER of 35.1% (99% CI [30.6, 38.5])

entries.text: The authors report that language modeling significantly reduced CER and WER relative to vocabulary-constrained beam search without an LM.
entries.condition: Offline omission analyses on copy-typing trials; the full system adds linguistic scoring to classifier probabilities and vocabulary constraints.

entries.text: HGA+LFS produced median code-word classification accuracy of 54.2% in the feature-comparison analysis.
entries.condition: 10-fold cross-validation on the most recent 10,682 isolated-target trials, 26 silently attempted NATO code words, HGA+LFS; 99% CI [51.6, 56.2].
entries.loc: Results | Discriminatory content in high-gamma activity and low-frequency signals; Fig. 3

entries.text: LFS alone outperformed HGA alone for code-word classification, and combining HGA+LFS outperformed either feature type alone.
entries.condition: 10-fold cross-validated classification of silently attempted NATO code words; single participant and ECoG array.
entries.loc: Results | Discriminatory content in high-gamma activity and low-frequency signals

entries.text: The reported chance accuracy for the Fig. 3 code-word classification comparison was 3.7%.
entries.condition: Fig. 3a; 10-fold cross-validation of silent NATO code-word classification using HGA, LFS, and HGA+LFS.

entries.text: NATO code words were classified more accurately than the corresponding English letter attempts, which the authors attribute to richer phonetic variability and longer utterances.
entries.condition: HGA+LFS; the most recent 29 silent attempts per each of 26 code words and 26 letters; 10-fold cross-validation.
entries.loc: Results | Differences in neural discriminability between NATO code words and letters

entries.text: Cross-type models achieved above-chance median accuracy of 36.3% when trained on silent attempts and tested on overt attempts, and 33.5% for the reverse direction.
entries.condition: 10-fold cross-validated HGA+LFS code-word classification; silent-train/overt-test CI [35.0, 37.5], overt-train/silent-test CI [31.0, 35.0]; stated chance 3.85%; matched-type training/testing performed significantly better.
entries.loc: Results | Distinctions in evoked neural activity between silent- and overt-speech attempts

entries.text: The body text reports a 3.85% chance baseline for silent/overt cross-type code-word classification; the Fig. 5 caption rounds it as 3.84%.
entries.condition: 26-class code-word classification in the silent-versus-overt comparison; internal rounding inconsistency between Results text and Fig. 5 caption.
entries.loc: Results | Distinctions in evoked neural activity between silent- and overt-speech attempts; Fig. 5 caption

entries.text: Attempted hand squeeze was classified with 98.43% accuracy for sentence termination.
entries.condition: Single participant; hand-motor command classified from ECoG and distinguished from silent-speech attempts; 99% CI [95.31, 99.22].
entries.quote: 98.43% classification accuracy (99% CI [95.31, 99.22])

entries.text: Offline copy-typing simulation with a 3,303-word vocabulary yielded median CER 7.18% and WER 12.4%.
entries.condition: Offline simulation of the real-time copy-typing blocks (34 blocks); n-gram LM retrained for the larger vocabulary; 99% CIs CER [2.25, 11.6], WER [8.01, 22.7].
entries.loc: Results | Generalizability to larger vocabularies and alternative tasks; Fig. 6

entries.text: Offline copy-typing simulation with a 5,249-word vocabulary yielded median CER 7.93% and WER 11.1%.
entries.condition: Offline simulation of the real-time copy-typing blocks (34 blocks); n-gram LM retrained for the larger vocabulary; 99% CIs CER [1.75, 12.1], WER [8.01, 23.1].
entries.loc: Results | Generalizability to larger vocabularies and alternative tasks; Fig. 6

entries.text: Offline copy-typing simulation with a 9,170-word vocabulary yielded median CER 8.23% and WER 13.3%.
entries.condition: Offline simulation of real-time copy-typing blocks (34 blocks); n-gram LM retrained; DistilGPT-2 unchanged; 99% CIs CER [2.25, 13.5], WER [7.69, 28.3].
entries.loc: Abstract; Results | Generalizability to larger vocabularies and alternative tasks

entries.text: No statistically significant difference in CER or WER was found among the tested vocabulary sizes; the >9,000-word result is offline, not real-time use.
entries.condition: Offline simulations reused the copy-typing neural predictions; the n-gram model was retrained for each vocabulary while final DistilGPT-2 was unchanged.
entries.quote: Overall, no significant differences were found between the CERs or WERs with any two vocabularies
entries.loc: Results | Generalizability to larger vocabularies and alternative tasks

entries.text: Conversational-task performance over the retained 28 trials was median CER 14.8% and WER 16.7%.
entries.condition: Real-time conversational task; 28 analyzed trials across 9 blocks, 2-4 responses per block; one participant; 99% CIs CER [0.00, 29.7], WER [0.00, 44.4].
entries.quote: Across 28 trials of this real-time conversational task condition, the median CER was 14.8% (99% CI [0.00, 29.7]) and the median WER was 16.7% (99% CI [0.00, 44.4])
entries.loc: Results | Generalizability to larger vocabularies and alternative tasks; Fig. 6

entries.text: For conversational ground truth, the participant confirmed exact outputs by nodding or entered the intended sentence using his commercial assistive-communication device.
entries.condition: Post-block self-report; non-perfect outputs were transcribed by the participant using his existing device.
entries.loc: Results | Assessing conversational task condition; Methods | Performance evaluation

entries.text: Copy-typing evaluation excluded 13 participant-reported error trials out of 163; retaining them raised median CER/WER to 8.52%/13.75%.
entries.condition: Copy-typing; participant reported using the wrong code word or losing his place; replacement attempts preserved two analyzed attempts per target sentence.
entries.quote: we excluded these trials (13 trials out of 163 total trials) from performance-evaluation analyses

entries.text: Conversational evaluation retained 28 of 39 original trials; trials were removed for getting lost, out-of-vocabulary words, or forgotten ground truth.
entries.value: 39 original; 28 analyzed; 2 lost; 6 OOV; 3 forgotten ground truth
entries.condition: Real-time conversational task; including OOV trials increased median CER/WER to 15.7%/17.6%.
entries.quote: Of 39 original conversational sentence-spelling trials, the participant got lost on 2 trials, tried to use an out-of-vocabulary word during 6 trials, and forgot the ground-truth sentence during 3 trials

entries.text: The authors explicitly characterize this as a single-participant pilot and require validation with more participants before clinical viability is established.
entries.condition: Generalization to other individuals and clinical conditions was not tested.
entries.quote: Additionally, the present results are limited to only one participant

entries.text: The authors concede that using multi-syllable code words is less natural than directly spelling letters and that fixed pacing limits user flexibility.
entries.condition: Current interface requires a code word per character at a predefined pace; flexible user-controlled pacing is future work.

entries.text: The interface did not let the participant retroactively edit the predicted sentence, although the language model could revise earlier words as later letters arrived.
entries.condition: Sentence-spelling interface during the reported task; corrections arose from decoder rescoring, not user edits.

entries.text: The authors claim that HGA and LFS contributed complementary, nonredundant information from relatively distinct cortical areas.
entries.condition: Feature-importance and spatial/temporal dimensionality analyses using the single participant's implanted ECoG array.
entries.loc: Results | Discriminatory content in high-gamma activity and low-frequency signals

entries.text: The authors call this the first BCI to combine speech-motor and hand-motor cortical areas for control.
entries.condition: Speech-motor signals decode characters; an attempted hand movement provides sentence termination.
entries.quote: Our approach is the first to combine the two cortical areas to control a BCI.

entries.text: The authors report continued stability of relevant cortical activity beyond 128 weeks after implantation.
entries.condition: Single participant and ECoG implant; stability claim is about relevant cortical activity, not a 128-week autonomous deployment trial.

entries.text: Clinical and regulatory requirements for the percutaneous connector prevented independent use of the current system.
entries.condition: Current implant has a percutaneous connector; independent use would require a fully implantable ECoG array and software integration with accessibility features.

entries.text: The authors propose possible use for people with complete vocal-tract paralysis, conditional on intact speech-motor cortex and the cognitive ability to attempt speech; they state further studies are needed.
entries.condition: Prospective extrapolation from one anarthric participant; complete vocal-tract paralysis was not studied in this paper.

entries.text: The article reports 10 distinct random initializations but does not report their seed values or an independent-seed replication schedule.
entries.condition: Sentence-spelling classifier ensemble; this is distinct from the 10-fold cross-validation procedure.
entries.quote: Specifically, we trained 10 separate classification models using the same training dataset and model architecture but with different random parameter initializations.
entries.loc: Methods | Classifier ensembling for sentence spelling

entries.text: The paper defines a randomized-probability chance condition but does not report its numerical sentence-level CER or WER in the text.
entries.condition: Offline simulation replacing classifier probabilities with random letter probabilities while retaining the rest of the pipeline; text reports only that errors were significantly worse than real-time results.

entries.text: The repository's example classifier split helper shuffles stratified samples with random_state=0; it splits trial rows rather than holding out entire sessions or blocks.
entries.condition: Code condition for the example classifier cross-validation helper; do not assume it is the split for every reported evaluation or the real-time copy-typing blocks.

entries.text: The example notebook configures a model-data cutoff before 2021-08-10 and demonstrates held-out inference on block 2726 recorded 2021-08-12; this is one example block, not all test blocks.
entries.condition: Repository example notebook's commented full-data recipe and worked realtime example; not a claim that all 34 evaluation blocks share this date.

entries.text: Hyperparameters were chosen on held-out validation datasets; sentence-spelling classifier training also used earlier sentences only when CER was zero.
entries.condition: Model hyperparameters fit before real-time testing; eligible previous-session sentence-spelling data required exact decoded text.
entries.loc: Methods | Modeling; Incremental classifier recalibration for sentence spelling

entries.text: The paper's main contribution is real-time sentence spelling from silent attempts to produce NATO code words, complementing prior direct full-word decoding.
entries.unit: English letters represented by code words
entries.condition: One participant; real-time spelling used the 1,152-word vocabulary; the greater-than-9,000-word results were offline simulations.

entries.text: The authors characterize silently attempted speech with implanted ECoG as an immediately practical, clinically viable spelling-BCI control modality, while noting that some patients may prefer it for naturalness.
entries.condition: Discussion-level clinical interpretation based on one participant; preference and robustness across patients were not directly tested in this study.
entries.loc: Discussion | Comparison with prior BCI approaches

entries.text: The authors suggest the attempted-hand-movement stop signal may be preferable to fixed-time termination, extraneous stopping, or head-movement termination used by prior spellers.
entries.condition: A proposed advantage; the paper did not experimentally compare stopping mechanisms across systems.

entries.text: The authors conclude that producing residual vocalizations is not necessary for attempted-speech control of this neuroprosthesis.
entries.condition: Shown with silent attempts in one participant; the participant could vocalize grunts and moans but produced no vocal output during spelling.

entries.text: Silently mouthed (subvocal) sEMG word sequences were recognized with four grammar models, one of them an unrestricted NATO grammar.
entries.condition: sEMG, subvocal speaking mode; HMM recognizer; word sequences from Corpus 2
entries.quote: Overall, four different grammar models were tested: sentence construction grammar, unrestricted NATO grammar, NL equivalence grammar, and unigram grammar.

entries.text: 4 subjects silently produced 1200 word sequences from a 202-word vocabulary that included the NATO alphabet.
entries.condition: sEMG, subvocal speech, healthy speakers; mean 6.0 words per phrase
entries.quote: A total of 4 subjects were presented with 1200 word-sequences (mean words/phrase = 6.0) generated from a relatively small 202-word vocabulary, including words and numbers associated with a special operations silent-speech data set (US Army 2009), the NATO alphabet and commonly used English phrases

entries.text: Intracortical typing used a Kalman-filter cursor and an HMM state classifier for discrete selection (click).
entries.condition: Intracortical microelectrode arrays, motor cortex; point-and-click keyboard

entries.text: Participant T5 averaged 39.2 correct characters per minute with the OPTI-II keyboard.
entries.condition: Intracortical point-and-click copy typing, participant T5, OPTI-II layout; mean ± s.d. 1.2

entries.text: Review: language models add a bias that can improve typing speed and accuracy in BCI spelling, and add word completion or automatic error correction.
entries.condition: Review of language-model integration in BCI spellers (mostly P300)
entries.quote: By exploiting known patterns and structures inherent in language, a bias can be added to a communication system which can improve typing speed and accuracy as well as adding other features such as word completion or automatic error correction.

entries.text: Review: word-based language methods are limited to words seen in training and generally cannot handle out-of-vocabulary words.
entries.condition: Review of BCI speller language models
entries.quote: One problem with these word based methods is that they are limited to the words that are seen during language model training and generally cannot handle out of vocabulary (OOV) words.

entries.text: An implanted intracortical speller in a completely locked-in ALS patient produced intelligible messages at 1.08 characters per minute on average.
entries.condition: Intracortical arrays; auditory-guided neurofeedback, yes/no letter selection; one patient

entries.text: The patient used an auditory-guided neurofeedback strategy to select letters and form words and sentences.
entries.condition: Intracortical speller, CLIS, eyes closed

entries.text: Raw online handwriting copy typing plateaued at 90 characters per minute with 5.4% character error rate.
entries.condition: Intracortical, one participant (T5), attempted handwriting, raw online output without language model, 31-character set, daily recalibration
entries.quote: typing rates were high, plateauing at 90 characters per minute with a 5.4% character error rate

entries.text: Attempted finger typing reached 110 characters per minute, 22 words per minute, 1.6% WER.
entries.condition: Intracortical, attempted finger typing (QWERTY), two participants, peak in one; user-regulated speed; 5-gram language model
entries.quote: Typing speed is user-regulated, reaching 110 characters per minute, resulting in 22 words per minute with a word error rate of 1.6%.

entries.text: Sentence decoding in the finger-typing BCI used a 5-gram language model.
entries.condition: Intracortical typing BCI
entries.quote: Sentence decoding is improved using a 5-gram language model.

entries.text: Later work in the same lineage separated attempted finger flexions from silent NATO code words in 569 of 570 test trials.
entries.condition: ECoG (253 channels), participant with anarthria, NATO-motor task, four finger-flexion targets
entries.quote: the model correctly classified 569 out of 570 test trials as either finger flexion or silent speech

entries.text: Later work classified the 26 silent NATO code words at 96.8% mean accuracy across 19 sessions after freezing the classifier.
entries.condition: ECoG, participant with anarthria, NATO-motor task, 99% CI [94.5, 98.6], frozen classifier trained on 1,196 trials

entries.text: An audio-visual recognizer decoded continuously spelled letter sequences (German alphabet) from lip images and audio; the authors describe the letter vocabulary as highly confusable.
entries.condition: Overt spelled letters, one camera, speaker-dependent; recognition, not a deployed speller
entries.quote: The task is thus equivalent to contiuous recognition with a small but highly confusable vocabulary.

entries.text: Visual-alone recognition of continuously spelled letters was 45-55%.
entries.condition: Continuous spelling task, visual-only (lip images), overt speech
entries.quote: On a continuous spelling task, visual-alone recognition of 45-55%

entries.text: SilentSpeller recognizes the 26 letters of the alphabet silently mouthed while spelling words, from an in-mouth capacitive sensor.
entries.condition: Electropalatography retainer, 124 capacitive electrodes; silent spelling of letter names; CHI 2022 (2022-04-29)
entries.quote: SilentSpeller focuses on recognizing the 26 letters of the alphabet, silently mouthed in the context of spelling a word.

entries.text: Live text entry with silent spelling averaged 37 words per minute at 87% accuracy over seven participants.
entries.condition: Live entry, electropalatography, 1164-word dictionary offline
entries.quote: Live text entry speeds for seven participants averaged 37 words per minute at 87% accuracy.

entries.text: Code words were classified more accurately than letters (Wilcoxon z = 3.78).
entries.condition: HGA+LFS, most recent 29 silent attempts per code word and per letter, 10-fold cross-validation, isolated targets, offline, one participant
entries.quote: Indeed, code words were classified with significantly higher accuracy than the letters (z = 3.78, P = 1.57 ×10−4, two-sided Wilcoxon Rank-Sum test; Fig. 4a).
entries.loc: Results / Differences in neural discriminability between NATO code words and letters; Fig. 4a

entries.text: Including the out-of-vocabulary conversational blocks raised median CER and WER to 15.7% and 17.6%.
entries.condition: Real-time conversational task; blocks with out-of-vocabulary attempts included; 99% CIs [6.25, 30.4] and [12.5, 45.5]
entries.quote: Incorporating blocks where the participant used intended words outside of the vocabulary only modestly raised CER and WER to median values of 15.7% (99% CI [6.25, 30.4]) and 17.6%, (99% CI [12.5, 45.5]) respectively.

entries.text: The authors compare with intracortical spelling at 90 characters per minute and note that participant could speak normally.
entries.condition: Discussion comparison with prior BCI approaches
entries.quote: recently achieving spelling rates as high as 90 characters per minute with a single participant, although this participant was able to speak normally
entries.loc: Discussion / Comparison with prior BCI approaches

entries.text: Applying a language model offline to the handwriting output gave 0.89% CER.
entries.condition: Offline 50,000-word bigram on raw online output, T5, five days
entries.quote: Online output + offline language model 0.89% [0.61, 1.2] 3.4% [2.5, 4.4]

entries.text: In click tasks participant T6 selected targets by squeezing her left hand; dwell tasks used holding the cursor still.
entries.condition: Intracortical cursor control, T6; click vs dwell selection
entries.quote: acquired targets by holding the cursor still over the target (dwell tasks) or squeezing her left hand (ipsilateral to the implanted array) when the cursor was over the target (click tasks)

entries.text: Peak rates were 47 characters per minute for T17 and 110 for T18.
entries.condition: Attempted finger typing, intracortical, peak over sessions
entries.quote: with T17 reaching a peak of 47 characters per minute and T18 reaching 110 characters per minute

questions.q: Were vocabularies larger than 1,152 words tested in live spelling?
questions.answer: No. Real-time sentence spelling used 1,152 words. The 3,303-, 5,249-, and 9,170-word results came from offline copy-typing simulations.

questions.q: How broad is the evidence for user-independent clinical viability?
questions.answer: The results are from one participant. The authors call for additional participants, and this participant could not use the current percutaneous system independently.

questions.q: Was there same-day recalibration during the reported real-time testing?
questions.answer: No. The article states models were fitted using preceding-session data and there was no day-of recalibration.

questions.q: What did the authors present as the main novelty of the control method?
questions.answer: Real-time spelling from silent attempted NATO code words, with an attempted hand movement to end the sentence; they also claim the first BCI combination of speech- and hand-motor cortical areas.

questions.q: Which earlier designs could falsify novelty of silent code-word spelling, beam search with a language model, and a hand-motor stop command?
questions.answer: Whole-wiki full-text check: NATO code words appear in earlier silent-speech sEMG work (Meltzner 2018, unrestricted NATO grammar over subvocal word sequences) but not as a speller; spelling BCIs at the target's time use evoked potentials or motor/cursor selection, with language models reviewed by Speier 2016; hand-motor click selection in Pandarinath 2017.

questions.q: Triage: does any neural study dated 2021 or earlier combine speech-motor decoding with a hand-motor command for control?
questions.answer: Full-text check over neural studies dated 2021 or earlier (hand-command pattern plus speech-decoding pattern): 5 matches, all reference-list or review mentions or separate participants (Kennedy 2015); none combines both in one control system.
